posts.post_text: We banned ChatGPT in our analytics department last month. Not because AI is bad — because nobody could explain where the numbers came from. When a regulator asks 'how did you arrive at this figure?' and the answer is 'GPT said so', you've got a compliance problem. The AI trust gap is real and growing.
posts.angle: High-value CRO post with three ICP prospects engaging — validate the compliance pain point around explainability, and add a sharp insight about trust being earned through auditability not accuracy
posts.draft_comment: The 'GPT said so' problem is real — and honestly it's not even about AI being wrong, it's about there being no trail to follow when someone pushes back. Regulators don't just want the right answer, they want to see the working. Most analytics tools haven't caught up to that yet, AI-powered or not. The question isn't whether the number is correct — it's whether you can defend it at 9am on a bad Tuesday.

posts.post_text: We spent 18 months building a Power BI dashboard that our finance team refuses to use. They still export everything to Excel and email it around. The building part was easy. Getting people to actually trust the numbers enough to quote them in a board meeting? That's the real challenge nobody talks about. Anyone else hit this wall?
posts.angle: ICP prospect COO frustrated with Power BI adoption — validate the trust gap as the real problem, not the tooling
posts.draft_comment: The dashboard was never the hard part. It's that the moment one number looks off — even once — finance goes straight back to the spreadsheet they built themselves and trust completely. That trust debt is almost impossible to pay back after the fact. How long did it take before people started questioning the numbers?

posts.post_text: Unpopular opinion: most operational dashboards are vanity projects. We had 47 KPIs on our ops dashboard. Nobody looked at it. Cut it to 5 metrics that actually drive decisions. Usage went from 10% to 85%. The problem with BI isn't the tools — it's that we measure everything and understand nothing.
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Director of Operations at Summit Group) engaging on dashboard overload — validate the 47-to-5 insight, add the 'why dashboards get bloated in the first place' layer, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: 47 KPIs is actually pretty common — it usually means the dashboard was built to satisfy stakeholders, not to drive decisions. The moment you flip that around and ask 'what would make someone change their behaviour tomorrow?' the list collapses fast. Curious what the 5 ended up being — and whether the people who wanted the other 42 ever noticed they were gone.

posts.post_text: Hot take: self-service BI is a myth. We gave everyone Power BI licenses and what happened? 200 reports, zero consistency, three different definitions of 'revenue'. The promise of democratising data is great until you realise nobody agrees on what the data means. Build vs buy isn't the question — it's 'who owns the truth?'
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Innovation Director at NorthStar Retail) engaging with a post about BI chaos — validate the 'who owns truth' framing with a sharper observation, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: The 200 reports thing is so real — and honestly the problem isn't the tool, it's that nobody agreed on definitions before the licences went out. Self-service BI just accelerates whatever mess already existed in the business. The question I keep hearing isn't 'who owns the truth' — it's 'who's allowed to change it when the business changes?'

posts.post_text: AI hallucinations in analytics are a security issue, not just an accuracy issue. If your AI tool generates a financial report with hallucinated numbers and someone makes a decision based on it, that's not a bug — it's a material risk. We need to start treating AI outputs with the same scrutiny as we treat user inputs.
posts.angle: CISO raising AI hallucinations as a material risk with a CEO ICP prospect engaging — validate the security framing, add the trust layer insight, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: The framing here is exactly right and I don't think most analytics vendors have caught up to it yet. There's a difference between a wrong number and an unverifiable number — and hallucinated outputs often look identical to correct ones, which is the actual problem. Most teams have no audit trail to even know when it happened. How are you currently thinking about what 'scrutiny' looks like in practice — is it process-side or are you expecting tooling to carry that weight?

posts.post_text: Had a fascinating conversation with a client yesterday. They spent £200k on a BI platform and the only person who can use it is the one who built it. Self-service my arse. The gap between what vendors promise and what actually happens in a 50-person company is enormous. When will the industry admit that most BI tools are built for data teams, not business teams?
posts.angle: ICP prospect (COO at Sterling Consulting) engaging with a post about BI tools failing non-technical users — validate the specific £200k waste pain, add the insight that self-service is a design problem not a training problem
posts.draft_comment: That £200k number is painfully common — and the punchline is usually the same: one person becomes the bottleneck, everyone else just emails them. The industry keeps solving for data teams because that's who evaluates the tools in the first place. Business users never get a seat in the demo, so it's no wonder the product doesn't fit them. Who actually signed off on the purchase — the data person or someone in ops?

posts.post_text: Just had our quarterly review and the CFO asked why the numbers in our BI dashboard don't match the numbers in the ERP. Turns out three different teams were applying different filters to the same dataset. AI won't fix this. Culture will. But nobody wants to hear that.
posts.angle: Commercial Director at a mid-market manufacturer hitting the classic 'whose numbers are right' wall — validate that this is a governance problem dressed up as a tech problem, not the other way around
posts.draft_comment: The filter thing is brutal because everyone's technically right — they're just answering slightly different questions with the same data. And that's not a dashboard problem, that's a 'we never agreed what revenue actually means in this context' problem. Culture is the right word but I'd narrow it even further: it's about who owns the definition. Has the CFO asked that question yet, or are they still pointing at the tool?

posts.post_text: Rolled out Copilot to 500 users last quarter. Usage after 90 days? 12%. The problem isn't the tool — it's that nobody knows what to ask it. We're essentially paying for a very expensive autocomplete. Shadow AI is the real story here — people are using ChatGPT on their phones because Copilot is too locked down.
posts.angle: IT Director surfacing the 'nobody knows what to ask' adoption failure — validate the root cause and reframe it as a data literacy problem, not a tool problem
posts.draft_comment: That 12% number is brutal but honestly not surprising. The assumption baked into most of these rollouts is that people already know what questions they need answered — they don't, and no amount of prompt coaching fixes that. Shadow AI on personal phones is the tell: people want help, they just want it to meet them where they are, not where the enterprise security policy is. What did your 12% actually have in common?
